actions.reason: No measurable encode_ir improvement found; both edits are reverted. (1) Moving the unicodedata import in base.py into replace_control_characters: encode_ir ratio 1.0007, so that import costs nothing in this bench. (2) Rewriting the pair scan in RegexTokenizer._encode_chunk with C builtins (zip/map over merges.get, then min/index/count): outputs identical, but encode_ir ratio 1.1852, because building and hashing a tuple per pair costs more than the nested-dict scan on the short cached chunks. The encode path already has the chunk cache, the in-place single merge and the lazy gpt4/tiktoken imports, so whatever remains looks like it needs profiling before another attempt.

journal.text:
I tried two changes aimed at encode_ir. First I moved the unicodedata import in minbpe/base.py into replace_control_characters. Second I rewrote the pair scan in RegexTokenizer._encode_chunk in minbpe/regex.py. The new scan used C builtins: zip and map over merges.get, then min, index and count.

The import move gave encode_ir 406816729 to 407106987, ratio 1.0007, and was rejected. That import costs nothing in this bench. The _encode_chunk rewrite kept outputs identical, but encode_ir went from 406816729 to 482157663, ratio 1.1852, and was rejected. train_ir moved only to ratio 0.9995. Neither change helped. Both are reverted and no candidate was submitted.

I now believe import cost is not where encode_ir goes. Swapping the Python loop in _encode_chunk for builtin chains made it slower, not faster.

Next I will profile _encode_chunk to see where the instructions go before I edit it. Then I will look at reducing the passes over ids per merge rather than swapping in builtins.
